name: Vitamin E oil / Bio-Oil

lead: Vitamin E oil and cosmetic scar oils such as the brand Bio-Oil are marketed and widely used with the idea that they help scars heal or fade. Proponents of such products often point to the antioxidant properties of vitamin E.
Reviews cited by Wikipedia have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for those claims, and its Scar article says research shows vitamin E to be ineffective for scars.

paras: Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant, and the proposed idea is that applying it to skin supports healing and limits scar tissue. Wikipedia reports reviews finding insufficient evidence to support this.

Wikipedia reports vitamin E causes contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and may worsen some scars, though another article notes allergy incidence is low despite widespread use. Products are sold over the counter.

lead: Vitamin E oil is topical tocopherol, a fat-soluble antioxidant applied to the skin, commonly with the aim of improving wound healing and reducing scar tissue. Bio-Oil is a commercial cosmetic oil product marketed for scars and stretch marks; the sources reviewed here do not describe it specifically.

Wikipedia's article on tocopherol states that topical vitamin E is widely used on skin and that reviews have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for claims that it improves wound healing or reduces scars [1]. Its article on scars says research shows vitamin E to be ineffective for scars, that it causes contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users, and that it may worsen some scars [2].

Allergic contact dermatitis has been linked to vitamin E derivatives such as tocopheryl linoleate and tocopherol acetate in skin-care products, although incidence is described as low considering the widespread use [1].
infobox: Tocopherol (vitamin E) and other oils, depending on product

paras: Topical vitamin E is sold as pure oil, in capsules that people puncture, and as an ingredient in creams. Branded scar oils are typically blends of vegetable oils and vitamins. The scar-oil category is distinct from silicone gels and sheets, which are the most studied non-prescription scar products [2].

Reviews have repeatedly concluded there is insufficient evidence that topical vitamin E speeds wound healing or reduces scarring [1]. The Scar article states that research shows vitamin E and onion extract to be ineffective for scars [2].

Vitamin E can cause allergic contact dermatitis [1]. Wikipedia's Scar article reports contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and that it may worsen some scars [2], while the tocopherol article describes incidence as low relative to how often the vitamin is used [1]. The two descriptions differ in emphasis.
No studies found specific to Bio-Oil in the sources reviewed here. Studies of topical vitamin E for scars are summarised in reviews that find insufficient evidence [1][2].
Vitamin E and Bio-Oil are commonly mentioned as inexpensive scar and skin-care products in appearance discussions. No community material is cited here.
